card.name: Gwoka
card.era: Originated 17th c. (slavery); rehabilitated post-1946 and from the 1960s-70s; UNESCO 2014
card.tagline: Guadeloupe's emblematic Afro-Creole drum, song and dance tradition.
card.profile: Gwoka is the umbrella Afro-Guadeloupean tradition combining responsorial singing in Guadeloupean Creole, rhythms played on the ka drums, and improvisational dance. It is generally played with three drums - two lower-pitched 'boula' carrying the central ostinato and one higher 'make'/marqueur (soloist) that dialogues with the dancer - accompanied by chacha (gourd rattle) and tibwa (sticks). Built on seven base rhythms, it is performed in the lawonn (circle) at the lewoz night gathering, where dancers enter one at a time to face the drums while the public claps and sings the chorus. It emerged on sugar, coffee and banana plantations and became a symbol of resistance and Guadeloupean identity (UNESCO; Repriz/ZoukJam).
card.insight: Gwoka was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List on 26 November 2014; ethnomusicologist Jerome Camal notes that because Guadeloupe is a French overseas department without a UN seat, the petition had to be sponsored by the French state, and the campaign was led from 2004 by Felix Cotellon of the centre Repriz (Camal, Intl Journal of Heritage Studies, 2016; UNESCO).
